reason: Attacked and survived, and the 1855 edition named in the source line is now actually opened rather than inferred from Gutenberg. Gutenberg 8642 has the sentence at line 4979, inside Part I (the essay runs from line 458 to line 5145), so the claim that it sits in the essay and not in the appended miscellanies holds. I then downloaded the scan of the Arthur B. Fuller edition itself, Internet Archive womaninnineteent00fulluoft, whose copyright page reads “Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1855, by A. B. Fuller”: the sentence stands on page 174, under the running head “174 WOMAN IN THE NINETEENTH CENTURY”, reading “I do not care what case you put ; let them be sea-captains, if you will.” The only difference is the French spacing before the semicolon, which is compositor practice and not wording. I also checked the 1845 first edition, womanintheninete00fulluoft, and the sentence is word for word identical there, so Arthur Fuller did not touch it and no edition choice is being hidden. Ends in a full stop; the hyphen in sea-captains is the text's own; prose kept as prose; no dash and no straight quote in the source line, 107 characters, leads with the name; tag Essay is the form of the work. shipped.js: not banned, zero of three, nothing shipped and nothing near. The one real weakness is the locator: the rule wants a chapter, section or line, or else an edition and a page, and “on the offices women may fill” is a descriptive phrase with an edition but no page. The essay has no chapter divisions, so the fix is the page, which I have now found. Ship it with p. 174 in the source line (116 characters).
betterCitation: Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, on the offices women may fill, p. 174 (ed. Arthur B. Fuller, 1855)
